definition: Shining or phosphorescent in the night; specifically used of the rare, high-altitude clouds that glow electric blue or silver after sunset in midsummer, visible only in the weeks around the solstice when the sun dips just below the horizon and still catches ice crystals fifty miles up.
etymology: From Latin nox, noctis, meaning night, and lucere, to shine — the same lucere that gave us lucid, translucent, and the name Lucifer, the light-bearer. The compound traveled into English through scientific Latin in the 1880s, coined precisely to describe these clouds when they were first formally studied. Night-shining: the word does exactly what it says.
usage: June is the prime window for spotting noctilucent clouds from northern latitudes — step outside an hour after sunset, look low toward the north, and if the sky offers a faint rippled silver-blue curtain hanging where darkness should be, you are seeing something noctilucent, a phenomenon so tied to the season that the word itself feels like a midsummer gift.
